verdicts.why: No bound is bypassed and nothing is allocated: java.util.Date(long) accepts the entire long range and Java defines the multiply as two's-complement wraparound, so an overflowing product only maps one peer-chosen 64-bit value onto another Date the same peer could have requested directly.

The claim itself states 'No security impact but poor practice' — swapping the literal "utf-8" for StandardCharsets.UTF_8 is a style/micro-optimization preference with no attacker and no behavioral difference (the charset lookup is cached and the method already declares IOException).

Whether available() can return 0 while table bytes remain depends entirely on TruncatedInputStream.available() and on the stream the caller hands to the ValueReader constructor (line 57); neither TruncatedInputStream.java nor any caller is present under the target path.

Same dependency as M03 for both loops: the generic InputStream.available() contract is quoted correctly, but deciding whether it under-reports for these specific streams requires TruncatedInputStream.java and the concrete stream passed in at line 57, which are outside the target files.

Factual error at the core of the claim: AMQP 0-9-1 encodes 'timestamp' as 64-bit POSIX time_t in SECONDS, so the *1000 at line 269 is exactly the seconds-to-milliseconds conversion java.util.Date requires — removing it, not keeping it, would produce dates off by 1000x.

The array at line 88 is allocated from the peer-supplied length BEFORE in.readFully() at line 89 verifies any data exists, and the only guard (line 87) admits everything below Integer.MAX_VALUE, so a 5-byte 'S' or 'x' field inside a table triggers a ~2GB allocation.

Could not refute: readBytes() is reachable from readFieldValue() cases 'S'/'x' (lines 162, 211) and from public readLongstr(), and line 87's 'contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE' is the only check, permitting a near-2GB allocation that precedes readFully — no enclosing bound exists in these files.

Identical dependency to M03/M04 for readArray: the arrayIn stream at line 241-242 wraps TruncatedInputStream, whose available() implementation is not among the target files, so the premature-zero premise cannot be confirmed or broken here.

The claim concedes its own refutation: the collections are filled only from the TruncatedInputStream-bounded streams (lines 146-147, 241-242), so every entry costs the attacker bytes actually delivered — and the stated scenario ('tableLength=2GB with thousands of tiny entries') yields only a few hundred KB of heap, while the duplicate-key guard at line 151 caps growth from repeated names; the suggested fix (HashMap initial capacity) would increase memory use, not reduce it.

The method returns Map<String,Object> (line 139), which cannot hold duplicate keys by definition, so a first-wins or last-wins policy is mandatory and the guard at line 151 is a deliberate choice, not data loss; no attacker gains anything from it.

Same as M10: the Map return type makes duplicate retention impossible, and 'an attacker might expect both values to be retained' describes no impact — if anything first-wins at line 151 is the conservative choice, since it prevents a later entry from overriding an earlier one. A missing log line is not a defect.

Could not refute: readFieldValue case 'F' calls readTable (line 181) and case 'A' calls readArray (line 184), both of which call readFieldValue again (lines 150, 245), with no depth counter anywhere in the file; each nesting level costs the sender only ~5-6 bytes, so a few tens of KB of input exhausts a default JVM stack.

unsignedExtend() masks with 0xffffffffL (lines 45-49), so a 'negative' int becomes a long in [2^31, 2^32-1] which fails the 'contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE' test at line 87 and throws — the masking is precisely what makes the guard safe, and no negative value can ever reach new byte[] at line 88.

Factually wrong: Groovy 2.4.21 (pom.xml:81) is a 2021 release of the 2.4 line, contradicting 'no security updates since 2016', and the groovy-maven-plugin execution (lines 613-635) only runs the in-repo generate_amqp_sources.groovy over the project's own spec JSON — no untrusted input, no attacker, and the claim concedes it is not shipped.

Could not refute: the mutual recursion readTable(139) -> readFieldValue(150) -> readTable(181) and readArray(237) -> readFieldValue(245) -> readArray(184) has no depth limit, and the TruncatedInputStream wrappers bound bytes, not nesting depth.

Both inputs are already bounded by the code: readUnsignedByte() at line 172 confines scale to [0,255] (never the dangerous negative/Integer.MIN_VALUE case) and the fixed 4-byte array at line 173 confines the unscaled value to 32 bits, so the BigDecimal holds at most 10 significant digits and its constructor performs no digit expansion — there is no resource consumption to exhaust.

1.2.13 (pom.xml:64) is the patched release of the 1.2 branch (it is where CVE-2023-6378/6371 were fixed), the claim names no CVE that actually affects it, and the dependency is test-scoped (pom.xml:439) with no attacker-reachable path — 'older branch than 1.4.x' is an upgrade preference, not a defect.
